records.name: Melanija
records.facts_used: The Senn–Salys dictionary pairs Lithuanian Melanija with Melanie. This belongs to the Melania family, derived from Greek melaina, “black, dark”. The dictionary gives a direct spelling correspondence; it does not establish the language through which each Lithuanian family adopted the name. The 1964 Yla–Salys calendar lists Melanija with the short forms Mela and Lana on 31 December. The exact full name also appears in the 1968 dictionary; both texts were reprinted in 1983. These records show a full name and its calendar short forms, without dating the beginning of Lithuanian use.

records.name: Mingailė
records.facts_used: Pakerys treats Mingailė as a Lithuanian compound feminine name. Its masculine counterpart Mingaila appears in Salys’s stem list under Min-, associated with minti and minėti, “remember, mention”. Salys associates Gail- with gailėti and gailus; these word links are not a single literal description of a bearer. In his 2011 study, Pakerys explicitly names Mingailė among the few compound feminine names already in the 1927 Jaunimo kalendorius. This is a dated historical calendar reference reported by the researcher. It does not claim that 1927 was the name’s creation year or its first birth registration.

records.name: Silver
records.facts_used: Rajandi discusses Estonian Silver as a short form of Silvester, whose Latin basis means “of the forest”. He also notes an English surname explanation from silversmith. These belong to different naming contexts and do not make the English word “silver” the automatic origin of every Estonian bearer’s name. The 1966 lexicon describes Silver as a short form returning to given-name use and records a historical frequency of one per thousand. That is the author’s period-specific observation, not a present-day bearer count. The same discussion also distinguishes older surname traces of the Silvester family.
